title: SciEx: Benchmarking Large Language Models on Scientific Exams with Human Expert Grading and Automatic Grading
extended_summary:
This paper does not study a ChatGPT mathematics intervention in grades 6–8. Instead, it introduces SciEx, a benchmark for evaluating large language models on university computer science exams. The motivation is to assess how well LLMs can solve scientific, free-form exam questions that resemble real university assessment rather than multiple-choice benchmarks.

The benchmark includes 10 exams from Karlsruhe Institute of Technology across several computer science courses, with questions in English and German and with both text-only and image-related items. The authors evaluate multiple LLMs, including GPT-4V, GPT-3.5, Claude, Llama3, Mixtral, Qwen, Mistral, and Llava, by having models answer the exam questions one at a time. Lecturers then grade the model outputs using the same criteria they use for students, and the paper also tests LLM-as-a-judge automatic grading against expert grades.

The main findings are that SciEx is challenging for current LLMs: the best examinee model, Claude, achieves 59.4% of the maximum score on average, though the strongest proprietary models can outperform the student average. The paper also finds that LLMs can act as reasonably reliable graders, with GPT-4V reaching 0.948 Pearson correlation with expert grading at the exam level. This is benchmark/evaluation research rather than an instructional intervention study, and it provides no direct evidence about grade 6–8 mathematics learning outcomes or counterfactual classroom effects.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed-style empirical benchmark study with human expert grading and quantitative comparison, but it is not a causal education intervention study and lacks a counterfactual instructional design. It is best classified as correlational/benchmark evidence rather than experimental evidence.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports meaningful performance and grading-quality benchmarks for LLMs, but it does not test a classroom intervention or demonstrate direct learner impact. Any educational impact is indirect and mainly relates to assessment efficiency rather than student outcomes.

interventions.use_case: Benchmarking large language models on free-form university computer science exam questions, including using LLMs as examinees and as automated graders (LLM-as-a-judge) rather than deploying an educational tutoring system.

finding.finding_summary: This is not a K-12 instructional intervention study; it benchmarks LLM performance on university computer science exam questions and compares LLM grades to student averages. The strongest models (Claude 59.4% and GPT-4V 58.2%) exceeded the student average (45.3%) on the exam-level score, but performance remained far from perfect and varied by language, difficulty, and modality.
finding.measure: Exam-level normalized grade (% of maximum points) on university computer science exams; also compared to student average grades
finding.study_size: n=1120 question-answer pairs from 7 LLMs across 154 questions in 10 exams

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that LLM-as-a-judge can automate grading with high agreement to expert grading, suggesting potential efficiency gains for assessment workflows. On exam-level grading, GPT-4V achieved Pearson correlation r=0.948 with expert grades, and Llama3 reached r=0.883; on question-level grading, correlations were around 0.7 in the best settings.
finding.measure: Pearson correlation between LLM grader and expert grader; question-level RMSE
finding.effect_size: r=0.948 (best exam-level correlation); question-level correlations around 0.7
